subtype: Approach: planning for the holidays with a neighbour [Thinking]
passage:
Friday
We leave for Mama's wedding in Lucknow on Monday, for a whole week. My plants! Seven pots on the balcony, all in different corners. I thought about who could water them. Jahnavi-didi downstairs loves gardening and is home in the evenings. But seven pots in seven corners is a lot to ask. So after school I dragged them all together near the balcony door, where the hose reaches and she won't have to walk around. Then I went down and asked her. She said yes! I wrote a small card: "Water every second evening. More for the tulsi, less for the cactus." Tomorrow I'll show her the pots so she isn't confused.
Himani

qa.q: How many pots does Himani have?
qa.a: Seven pots.

qa.q: What was Himani worried about?
qa.a: Himani was worried about the plants drying out and about asking too much of Jahnavi-didi.

qa.q: What else could Himani do before Monday?
qa.a: Himani could give every pot a good soak on Sunday night, so the first days are easy even if an evening is missed.

qa.q: What is the arrangement like for Jahnavi-didi?
qa.a: Much easier: the pots are together near the hose, and the card tells her exactly what each one needs.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child arranging for a neighbour to water the plants during a trip and grouping the pots to make it easier.

subtype: Approach: planning for the holidays with a neighbour [Thinking]
passage: The whole family was going to Sabina's Phuphi's village for a week of harvest, and her marigolds and chillies would be left behind. Sabina sat on the charpai counting: five pots by the gate, two on the roof, one near the cowshed. "Nobody will climb to the roof every day," she thought. "And nobody walks past the cowshed." On Sunday she carried all eight pots to the shaded wall beside the handpump, where anyone filling water would pass them. Then she walked across the lane to Deepika-bhabhi, who fetched water from that pump every morning. "Could you tip one lota on each when you fill your pots?" Deepika-bhabhi laughed. "Put them there, and how can I forget?" Sabina tied a red thread round the chilli pot, the thirstiest one.

qa.q: How many pots were on the roof?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: What was Sabina thinking on the charpai?
qa.a: She was worried that nobody would climb to the roof or walk past the cowshed, so she wanted the care made easy.

qa.q: What else could Sabina do if the week turned very hot?
qa.a: She could ask Deepika-bhabhi to give the red-thread chilli pot an extra lota, since it dries fastest.

qa.q: How does Deepika-bhabhi see the arrangement?
qa.a: Deepika-bhabhi is amused and happy to help, since the pots sit right where she fetches water.

grounding: A girl plans for a week away by grouping her pots by the handpump and asking a neighbour who passes daily to water them.

subtype: Approach: making a feeding and cleaning schedule [Action]
passage: I'm Madhav, Ujjwal's cousin, and I stayed at their place the week they got Moti. For the first two days nobody knew who had fed the puppy. Ujjwal's mother fed Moti, then his father fed Moti again, and then nobody filled the water bowl. On the third evening Ujjwal sat at the dining table with a sketch pen and a sheet of paper. He wrote: FOOD 7 am and 6 pm. WALK after school. WATER BOWL check morning and night. Beside each line he drew little boxes for the days. He pinned it to the board by the front door, right where you take off your shoes. After that, whoever fed Moti ticked a box. I don't know if Ujjwal was proud, but he checked that sheet every time he came in.

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal pin the sheet?
qa.a: On the board by the front door, where you take off your shoes.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal make the sheet?
qa.a: He seemed worried that Moti was being fed twice or left without water, and wanted the care to be steady.

qa.q: What else could help the schedule work?
qa.a: Writing a name beside each job, so everyone knows whose turn it is as well as what needs doing.

qa.q: How does Madhav see Ujjwal after the sheet?
qa.a: Madhav notices Ujjwal checking it every time he comes in, but is not sure whether Ujjwal feels proud.

grounding: A cousin watches a boy write a feeding, walking and water schedule for a new puppy and pin it by the door.

subtype: Approach: making a feeding and cleaning schedule [Action]
passage:
Saturday: The puppy arrived in a cardboard box. Mridul's father, Pankaj, fed her at breakfast; so did Dadi; so did Mridul after lunch. By evening the puppy had been sick on the rug.
Sunday: Mridul took a sheet of chart paper and wrote in big letters: FOOD, 7 in the morning and 6 in the evening. WALK, after school. WATER BOWL, check whenever you pass. He drew a column of boxes for each day and pinned it next to the front door, where everyone looks for keys.
Three weeks later: Pankaj came home late, glanced at the chart, saw the six o'clock box already ticked in Mridul's handwriting and put the food packet away. The puppy, fed once and walked, was asleep by nine.

qa.q: What happened on Saturday evening?
qa.a: The puppy had been sick on the rug.

qa.q: What might Mridul have felt when the puppy was sick?
qa.a: Worried and a bit guilty, since everyone, including him, had fed her.

qa.q: What else could the family try along with the chart?
qa.a: Keep the food in one place beside the chart, so nobody feeds the puppy without seeing the ticks.

qa.q: What is the chart like for Pankaj three weeks later?
qa.a: Pankaj can see at a glance that the evening feed is done, so he does not feed the puppy again.

grounding: Across three weeks, a boy's feeding and walking chart by the door stops the family overfeeding their new puppy.

subtype: Approach: observing the animal's behaviour to understand needs [Thinking]
passage:
"Ammi, Billo didn't eat her breakfast. Or last night's dinner."
"She's sulking, Zeenat. We moved her basket."
"But she's under the bed, right at the back. She never goes there."
Her sister Yamini looked up from her book. "Cats hide. That's what cats do."
"Not Billo. Billo sits on the fridge and yells for fish. And she didn't even come out when I opened the tin." Zeenat's voice wobbled. "If she was sulking, she'd still sniff it. She'd be cross, not hiding."
Ammi put down the ladle and crouched beside her. Two green eyes glowed from the dark, and the cat didn't move.
"You're right. That's not like her."
"Can you call the vet? Please? Today?"
Ammi was already reaching for her phone.

qa.q: Where was Billo hiding?
qa.a: Under the bed, right at the back.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's wobbling voice suggest?
qa.a: She was worried and frightened that something was really wrong with Billo.

qa.q: What else could Zeenat do while waiting for the vet?
qa.a: She could note when Billo last ate and whether she is drinking, so the family can tell the vet clearly.

qa.q: How does Ammi's view change?
qa.a: Ammi first says Billo is sulking, then sees the cat for herself, agrees it's not like her, and calls the vet.

grounding: A girl notices her cat hiding and not eating, decides it is more than sulking and asks her mother to call the vet.

subtype: Approach: observing the animal's behaviour to understand needs [Thinking]
passage: Last winter our cat, Mishti, stopped eating. I'm Himani. For two days she hid inside the cupboard among the old blankets. My brother Tejas said she was angry because we'd brought home a new sofa. I almost believed him. But I kept thinking: when Mishti is angry, she turns her back and flicks her tail. She doesn't hide, and she never skips fish. This was different. So I told Ma, "I don't think she's cross. I think she's hurting." Ma rang the vet that afternoon. The vet found a sore in Mishti's mouth that made eating painful, and treated it. A week later Mishti was back on the sofa, the new one, eating like a queen.

qa.q: Where did Mishti hide?
qa.a: Inside the cupboard among the old blankets.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when Tejas blamed the sofa?
qa.a: Himani almost believed him but felt uneasy, because the signs didn't match an angry Mishti.

qa.q: What else could Himani have watched for?
qa.a: Whether Mishti was drinking and moving normally, since that would help the vet and show how serious it was.

qa.q: How might Tejas see things now?
qa.a: Tejas guessed anger about the sofa; the vet finding a sore may show him that hiding can mean pain.

grounding: Looking back, a child reads a cat's hiding and not eating as a sign of trouble rather than sulking and gets a parent to call the vet.

subtype: Approach: enthusiasm early and neglect later [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Preeti, Vijay's older sister, and I've watched the whole rabbit story. Vijay begged for months. When Ruby finally came home, he was up at six to give her carrot tops, cleaned her cage every evening and read a library book about rabbits. For two weeks he talked of nothing else. In the third week he started saying, "After this match." By the fourth week it was Papa who crouched by the cage with the pellets before work, and Mummy who swept out the droppings at night. Yesterday Vijay walked past the cage with his bat and didn't even look. Ruby pressed her nose to the bars. Papa said nothing, but I saw him sigh.

qa.q: How long did Vijay care for Ruby eagerly?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What might Vijay have been feeling by the fourth week?
qa.a: His excitement had faded; he seemed bored with the routine and more interested in cricket.

qa.q: What else could the family try to keep Vijay involved?
qa.a: A small daily chart with Vijay's name on a few jobs, done before cricket, so the care stays his.

qa.q: What is Ruby's care like for Papa now?
qa.a: Papa feeds Ruby before work and seems tired or disappointed, sighing without saying anything.

grounding: A sister watches a boy care eagerly for a new rabbit for two weeks, then lose interest until the parents do the feeding.

subtype: Approach: enthusiasm early and neglect later [Pitfall]
passage:
First week of June: Nikita finally got her rabbit, a white one she named Rasmalai. She brushed her twice a day and showed her off to her friend Jasleen on a video call.
Mid-July: School had started again, and Nikita had dance class twice a week. "Mumma, can you feed her today? Just today?" turned into most days. Papa bought a bigger bag of pellets and began filling the bowl before his office bus.
End of August: Nikita came home and found Papa cleaning the cage on the terrace, sleeves rolled up. Rasmalai was nibbling hay he had put out. Nikita stood at the door for a long moment. Papa didn't scold. He just held out the brush.

qa.q: What did Nikita name the rabbit?
qa.a: Rasmalai.

qa.q: What might Nikita have felt standing at the door?
qa.a: Guilty and uncomfortable, seeing Papa doing the work she had promised to do.

qa.q: What else could Nikita try now that school is busy?
qa.a: Agree with Papa on one or two fixed jobs she can manage, such as the morning pellets, and tick them on a chart.

qa.q: What might Papa be feeling as he holds out the brush?
qa.a: Patient, perhaps a little tired; he does not scold but invites her back into the care.

grounding: Over three months, a girl's early enthusiasm for her rabbit fades and her parents end up feeding it.

subtype: Approach: asking an expert about the right food [Action]
passage:
Clinic note, Saturday.
Sachin, who looks about ten, came in with his parents and a six-week-old puppy. Before I could start the check-up, he pulled out a folded paper and asked, "What can she eat? Can she have chocolate? Our leftovers?" I explained that chocolate is unsafe for dogs and that spicy, oily leftovers can upset her stomach. He wrote each thing down, spelling "chocolate" very carefully. I suggested puppy food, and plain rice with a little boiled chicken as a treat, and his mother asked about timings. While his parents paid, Sachin was already drawing a table: morning, afternoon, night, with a name beside each. I have given the family our feeding handout.
Ankita, veterinary clinic

qa.q: What did Sachin pull out before the check-up?
qa.a: A folded paper with his questions.

qa.q: What does Sachin spelling 'chocolate' carefully suggest?
qa.a: He felt serious and responsible, eager to get the puppy's food right.

qa.q: What else could Sachin do when unsure about a new food later?
qa.a: Check the clinic's handout or ask the vet before giving it, rather than guessing.

qa.q: How might Sachin's parents benefit from his table?
qa.a: The whole family can see who feeds the puppy when, so the meals stay regular and safe.

grounding: A vet's note records a boy asking what his puppy can safely eat and planning its meals with his parents.

subtype: Approach: asking an expert about the right food [Action]
passage:
Wednesday
Today the vet came to the free animal camp on our school field, and I carried Tora there in my arms. Last week Jaya fed her a bit of birthday cake with chocolate icing, and Tora was sick all night. At home we give her whatever is left from dinner, even fish curry with chillies. The vet said chocolate is not safe for dogs at all, and spicy leftovers can hurt their stomachs. I felt bad about the curry. At home I sat with Ma and Deuta and made a meal plan on the back of an old calendar: puppy food morning and evening, a little plain rice and boiled egg sometimes, NO chocolate, NO chilli. Jaya drew a crossed-out cake at the bottom.
Bhupen

qa.q: What did Jaya feed Tora last week?
qa.a: A bit of birthday cake with chocolate icing.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel after the vet spoke?
qa.a: Bhupen felt bad, guilty about the spicy curry they had been giving Tora.

qa.q: What else could the family do to keep Tora safe?
qa.a: Keep chocolate and spicy food out of Tora's reach and tell visitors about the plan too.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel now?
qa.a: Jaya may feel guilty about the cake, but joins in by drawing the crossed-out cake on the plan.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child asking a vet about safe food for a puppy and making a meal plan with the parents.

subtype: Approach: learning from a mistake with the pet [Revision]
passage:
Class 6 pets corner, note by the class teacher.
Manjula looks after our class goldfish tank. On Monday she came to me looking worried: the two fish were gasping at the surface, and the glass felt warm. She had moved the tank to the window ledge last week "so they get sunlight". We checked the small tank thermometer together; it read well above the safe range written on the tank's label. She said quietly, "It's the sun. My mistake." Before I could suggest anything, she asked two classmates to help carry the tank to the shaded corner by the cupboard. Then she added a new line to her daily card: "Thermometer reading: ___." By Wednesday the fish were swimming normally again.
Dilnaz, class teacher

qa.q: Where had Manjula put the tank last week?
qa.a: On the window ledge.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel when she said 'My mistake'?
qa.a: She felt guilty and worried, but took responsibility straight away.

qa.q: What else could Manjula watch each day besides the thermometer?
qa.a: Whether the fish gasp at the surface, since that was the first warning sign this time.

qa.q: How did things change for the class by Wednesday?
qa.a: The fish were swimming normally again, so the class saw the problem noticed and fixed.

grounding: A teacher's note records a girl noticing her fish tank had overheated in the sun, moving it to shade and adding temperature checks.

subtype: Approach: learning from a mistake with the pet [Revision]
passage:
Sunday
I nearly cooked my fish. That's what Sarita-didi said, and she's right. Last week I moved the tank next to the balcony door because the light made the water sparkle. Today at lunchtime Bubbles and Pepper were hanging at the top, hardly moving, and the glass felt warm like bathwater. I felt sick. Didi and I pulled the curtain and carried the tank to the corner by the bookshelf, where the sun never comes. I stuck Papa's old aquarium thermometer inside. From now on my morning check has three things: food, filter, and the thermometer number, written in my pet notebook. By evening they were chasing each other again.
Rajni

qa.q: Where did Rajni move the tank to?
qa.a: The corner by the bookshelf, where the sun never comes.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel on touching the warm glass?
qa.a: Rajni felt sick with worry and guilt about moving the tank into the sun.

qa.q: What else could Rajni do in the hottest months?
qa.a: Rajni could check the thermometer in the afternoon as well, since the room may warm up later in the day.

qa.q: How did Sarita-didi react?
qa.a: She teased that Rajni nearly cooked the fish, but helped carry the tank to safety.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child moving a sun-warmed fish tank into shade and adding a thermometer reading to daily checks.

subtype: Approach: training through small rewards and repetition [Action]
passage: I'm Tushar. Pranav lives in the flat above ours, and every evening at six I see him on the colony lawn with Kaalu, their black dog. He does the same thing for about five minutes. He holds a tiny piece of dog biscuit over Kaalu's nose, moves it back, says "Sit", and the second Kaalu's bottom touches the grass, Pranav gives him the piece and scratches his ears. The first week Kaalu sat maybe half the time. Pranav didn't shout once. In the second week he started saying "Sit" without moving his hand. Only when Kaalu got that right did he try it with other dogs around. Now Kaalu sits at the gate before every walk. I don't know how Pranav stayed so patient.

qa.q: What time does Pranav train Kaalu?
qa.a: Every evening at six.

qa.q: What does Pranav never shouting suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He seems calm and patient, and determined to keep going even when Kaalu gets it wrong.

qa.q: What else could Pranav try if Kaalu gets distracted by other dogs?
qa.a: Go back to the quiet lawn for a few days and add the distractions slowly, the same step-by-step way.

qa.q: How does Tushar see Pranav's patience?
qa.a: Tushar is impressed, and a little puzzled about how Pranav stayed so patient. 🐕

grounding: A neighbour watches a boy teach his dog to sit with small treats in short daily sessions, making it harder only after success.

subtype: Approach: training through small rewards and repetition [Action]
passage:
Day one: Hemant's new puppy, Chikki, would not sit. Hemant pressed her back down and she wriggled away. His friend Deepak, who had trained two dogs, said, "Tiny treats. Every time she gets it right. Five minutes, no more."
Day ten: Every evening after homework, Hemant knelt on the verandah with a pocket of dried liver bits. "Sit." Chikki sat. Treat. "Sit." Chikki sat. Treat. When she did it five times in a row, he tried it standing up instead of kneeling.
Day thirty: Hemant said "Sit" in the busy lane outside, with a scooter going past. Chikki sat and looked up at him. He gave her the treat and a hug, and Deepak clapped from his gate.

qa.q: How long did Deepak suggest training each time?
qa.a: Five minutes, no more.

qa.q: How might Hemant have felt on day one?
qa.a: Frustrated, when Chikki kept wriggling away from his hand.

qa.q: What would you change if Chikki had failed in the busy lane?
qa.a: Go back to the step that worked, like standing on the quiet verandah, and try the lane again later.

qa.q: How does Deepak see Hemant's progress?
qa.a: Deepak is pleased and proud, clapping from his gate.

grounding: Over a month, a boy trains his puppy to sit with small rewards and short daily practice, adding difficulty only after success.

subtype: Approach: thinking of the pet as a family member with rights [Thinking]
passage: The snow had melted in Sapporo, and after school Aiko wanted to stay at the park until the lamps came on. "One more round of tag, Yuki!" Yuki checked the clock tower. Half past four. She thought of Kuro, their old dog, lying by the door since morning with only his food bowl for company. "Food isn't the whole thing," she thought. "If someone fed me and left me alone all day, I'd go strange too." She told Aiko, "I can't. Kuro's been alone all day. He needs his walk, and he needs someone to talk to." Aiko pouted. "He's a dog." "He's our dog," Yuki said, picking up her bag. At home, Kuro's tail thumped against the floor before she even opened the door.

qa.q: What time did Yuki see on the clock tower?
qa.a: Half past four.

qa.q: What was Yuki thinking about Kuro?
qa.a: She felt concerned for Kuro, alone all day, and reasoned that he needs walks and company, not just food.

qa.q: What else could Yuki try so she can still play sometimes?
qa.a: Bring Kuro to the park with her friends, so he gets his walk and she still gets her game.

qa.q: How does Aiko see Yuki leaving?
qa.a: Aiko pouts, disappointed, and seems to think a dog should not come before play.

grounding: A girl reasons that her dog needs walks and company as well as food, so she leaves the park early.

subtype: Approach: thinking of the pet as a family member with rights [Thinking]
passage: At the end of badminton practice at the sports club, the coach said the court was free till seven for anyone who wanted to stay. Pooja was already bouncing. "Parul, doubles! Come on!" Parul looked at the big clock over the scoreboard. Six. Both her parents worked late on Thursdays. Lucky had been in the flat since two, with food and water but nobody to lean against. "He eats fine," she thought, "but he's a dog, not a plant. He needs a walk and someone around." She zipped her racket bag. "Not today, Pooja. Lucky's waiting, and he's been alone all afternoon." Pooja groaned, then said, "Saturday, then?" "Saturday morning. I'll bring him to watch."

qa.q: When do both of Parul's parents work late?
qa.a: On Thursdays.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling as she zipped her bag?
qa.a: A little sorry to miss doubles, but responsible and sure Lucky needed her.

qa.q: What else could Parul arrange for Thursdays?
qa.a: She could ask a neighbour to take Lucky for a short walk, so she can sometimes stay late.

qa.q: How does Pooja react?
qa.a: Pooja groans at first, then accepts and suggests Saturday instead.

grounding: A girl turns down extra play at the club because her dog needs a walk and company, not just food.

subtype: Approach: forcing a frightened animal to play [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Rekha, and the kitten lives in the flat next to ours, with Vishal's family. The first evening it hid under their sofa, ears flat, tail puffed. Vishal kept lying on the floor, reaching under and pulling it out to cuddle. Each time it went stiff in his arms and made a low noise I'd never heard a kitten make. His mother said, "Let it come to you." He said, "But it's so soft." On the third evening I was at their door when the kitten twisted, scratched a long red line down Vishal's wrist and shot back under the sofa. Vishal stared at his wrist. His mother cleaned the scratch and put a plaster on it. I think he was more hurt that the kitten didn't like him, but I can't be sure.

qa.q: What did Vishal's mother do about the scratch?
qa.a: She cleaned it and put a plaster on it.

qa.q: What might Vishal be feeling as he stares at his wrist?
qa.a: Hurt and perhaps rejected, confused that the kitten did not want his cuddles.

qa.q: What else could Vishal have done the first evening?
qa.a: Sit quietly nearby and let the kitten come out by itself, treating flat ears and a puffed tail as signs to wait.

qa.q: What might the evenings be like for the kitten?
qa.a: Frightening: it was pulled out again and again while its whole body was saying 'leave me alone'.

grounding: A neighbour watches a boy keep picking up a frightened kitten, ignoring its signals, until it scratches him.

subtype: Approach: forcing a frightened animal to play [Pitfall]
passage:
Friday: The rescue kitten arrived at Tushar's house trembling in a basket. Tushar scooped it out at once and held it to his chest. It went rigid and its ears pressed flat. His cousin Tarun said, "Put it down, it's scared." "It just needs love," said Tushar.
Saturday: Tushar picked the kitten up six times. By evening it had learnt to run under the bed whenever he came in. The seventh time, it hissed, lashed out and left three thin scratches on his hand.
Wednesday: Tushar sat on the floor with a book, not looking at the kitten, a bowl of food beside him. It watched from under the bed for twenty minutes, then crept out and sniffed his sock. He kept very still. It stayed.

qa.q: How many scratches did the kitten leave?
qa.a: Three thin scratches.

qa.q: What did Tushar believe the kitten needed on Friday, and how did he feel?
qa.a: He believed it just needed love, and felt eager and affectionate, missing that it was scared.

qa.q: What worked on Wednesday, and why?
qa.a: Sitting still, not looking at the kitten and leaving food nearby, because it let the kitten choose when to come close.

qa.q: What was Saturday like for the kitten?
qa.a: Frightening; it learnt to run under the bed and finally lashed out when picked up again.

grounding: Over several days, a boy who keeps picking up a nervous kitten gets scratched, then learns to let it come to him.

subtype: Approach: planning for the pet during travel [Thinking]
passage: Three days before the family left Bengaluru for Kolkata, Madhav stood in front of the balcony cage where Mitthu and Hira, the two budgies, were squabbling over a millet spray. "Who feeds you when we're gone?" he said aloud. Last time Papa had remembered at the airport and made frantic calls. So Madhav went across the corridor to Chinmay-uncle, who kept a parrot of his own. "Could you feed our budgies for four days?" Uncle agreed. That evening Madhav wrote a card and taped it to the cage: "Seeds: one small cup in the morning. Water: change daily. Cover the cage at night. Keep out of the sun." On the morning they left, he handed Uncle the spare key and the card, and nobody made any calls from the airport.

qa.q: For how many days would Chinmay-uncle feed the budgies?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: What was Madhav thinking as he looked at the cage?
qa.a: He was worried about a repeat of last time, when Papa remembered only at the airport.

qa.q: What else could Madhav add to the card?
qa.a: A family phone number, so Chinmay-uncle can reach them if a bird seems unwell.

qa.q: How does the plan feel to Chinmay-uncle?
qa.a: Easy: he has the key and clear written steps, so he isn't left guessing.

grounding: Before a trip, a child thinks about who will feed the birds, arranges a neighbour and writes instructions on a card.

subtype: Approach: planning for the pet during travel [Thinking]
passage:
"Ankita, can I ask you something big?"
"How big?"
"We're going to Nashik for Diwali, five days. Who'll feed Chiku and Piku?"
"Your lovebirds? Can't your Aaji?"
"Aaji's coming with us. I only thought of it last night, lying in bed. If I don't sort it now, we'll remember in the car."
"Okay. What do I have to do?"
"I wrote it on a card. Look: seeds in the morning, fresh water, a piece of guava every second day, cover the cage at night because of the cold."
"Every second day? I'll forget."
"I drew a guava on those days on the calendar. Just match it."
"Madhuri, you've thought of everything."
"Not everything. I'm still worried the firecrackers will scare them."
"I'll keep the balcony door shut. Deal?"
"Deal."

qa.q: How long will the family be away?
qa.a: Five days, in Nashik for Diwali.

qa.q: What is Madhuri still worried about?
qa.a: Madhuri is worried the firecrackers will frighten the birds.

qa.q: What else could Madhuri do before leaving?
qa.a: Do one practice feed with Ankita, so any confusion shows up before the trip.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel about the job?
qa.a: Unsure at first about remembering, then reassured by the card and the guava calendar. 🙂

grounding: A child plans ahead for the family's birds during a family trip, arranging a friend to feed the birds and writing clear instructions.
